stemMd:
Readers who expect a memoir composed four decades after the events it describes to be **(i)** ______ will find this one disconcerting: its author sets down the townspeople's daily improvisations during the siege with **(ii)** ______ that betrays no knowledge of how the affair would end.

**Blank (i):** coloured by hindsight / hostile to its subject / meagre in detail

**Blank (ii):** detachment / immediacy / erudition
instructionsMd: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices. All blanks must be correct; there is no credit for a partially correct answer.
explanationMd:
Do the blank the sentence *defines* first, then use it to fix the other. Here that order is (ii) before (i).

**Blank (ii).** The relative clause is a gloss: the author writes in a way "that betrays no knowledge of how the affair would end." A memoirist obviously knows how the siege ended — he is writing forty years later — so the clause is describing a quality of the *writing*: it reads as though the outcome were still open, as though events were unfolding now. **"Immediacy"** names precisely that quality.

**Blank (i).** The sentence is built on a thwarted expectation: readers who expect (i) "will find this one disconcerting." So (i) must be the normal expectation that immediacy defeats. What a long retrospect normally produces is writing shaped by knowing the outcome — the siege narrated as inevitable, every improvisation read in the light of what it led to. **"Coloured by hindsight"** is that expectation, and immediacy is exactly its absence.

**The answer is "coloured by hindsight" and "immediacy."**

**How to check.** Read the completed sentence and confirm the two choices are in genuine tension, because "will find this one disconcerting" promises a surprise. *Expected: coloured by hindsight. Found: immediacy.* Those are opposites, so the surprise is real. Then check the other direction: if you can pair your two choices and the sentence produces no surprise at all, one of them is wrong even if each reads acceptably on its own. Because the item is scored all-or-nothing, spend your last few seconds on whichever blank you were less sure of.

distractorRationale.blank1-b: "Hostile to its subject" is not the expectation that four decades of distance creates, and immediacy is not its opposite. A hostile memoir could be written with great immediacy, so this choice leaves "disconcerting" with no surprise to announce.
distractorRationale.blank1-c: "Meagre in detail" would be defeated by abundance of detail, not by immediacy, and the sentence in fact reports detail — the townspeople's daily improvisations — without ever suggesting that readers expected the book to be thin.
distractorRationale.blank2-a: "Detachment" means emotional or critical distance. It is compatible with knowing exactly how the affair ended — a detached historian writes from the far side of the outcome — so it cannot explain the clause about betraying no knowledge of the ending, and it would confirm rather than confound the expectation the sentence sets up.
distractorRationale.blank2-c: "Erudition" means deep learning. Nothing in the sentence concerns the author's scholarship or range of reference, and a learned account would still reveal, rather than conceal, the writer's knowledge of how the siege turned out.

accessibilityText: A sentence with two blanks. Readers who expect a memoir composed four decades after the events it describes to be blank one will find this one disconcerting, colon, its author sets down the townspeople's daily improvisations during the siege with blank two that betrays no knowledge of how the affair would end. For blank one choose among coloured by hindsight, hostile to its subject, and meagre in detail. For blank two choose among detachment, immediacy, and erudition. All blanks must be correct; there is no credit for a partially correct answer.

provenance.notes: Original two-blank Text Completion written for the wave 4 top-up. Option ids are prefixed blank1- and blank2- so the renderer can group each column, and the answer key carries the full option id with a matching columnId. Blank (ii) is fixed by an explicit gloss and blank (i) by the thwarted-expectation frame, so neither blank can be solved by tone alone. Not adapted from any ETS item.

review.notes: Author solved as 'coloured by hindsight' and 'immediacy'. Blank (ii): the gloss 'betrays no knowledge of how the affair would end' describes writing that reads as if the outcome were still open, which is immediacy; detachment is compatible with full knowledge of the outcome and erudition is off-topic. Blank (i): 'will find this one disconcerting' requires the expectation to be the opposite of what is found, and the opposite of immediacy in a forty-year retrospect is writing coloured by hindsight; hostility and thinness of detail are not defeated by immediacy. Uniqueness checked pairwise across all nine combinations. Awaiting blind independent solve; the author must not publish own work.
